Amazon S3 	– 	Lifecycle Rules
• 	Transition Actions – configure objects to transition to another storage class
• 	Move objects to Standard IA class 60 days after creation
• 	Move to Glacier for archiving after 6 months
• 	Expiration actions – configure objects to expire (delete) after some time
• 	Access log files can be set to delete after a 365 days
• 	Can be used to delete old versions of files (if versioning is enabled)
• 	Can be used to delete incomplete Multi-Part uploads
• 	Rules can be created for a certain prefix (example: s3://mybucket/mp3/*)
• 	Rules can be created for certain objects Tags (example: Department: Finance)
© Stephane Maarek
NOT FOR DISTRIBUTION © Stephane
 Maarek
 www.datacumulus.com
Amazon S3 	– 	Lifecycle Rules (Scenario 1)
• 	Your application on EC2 creates images thumbnails after profile photos
are uploaded to Amazon S3. These thumbnails can be easily recreated,
and only need to be kept for 60 days. The source images should be able
to be immediately retrieved for these 60 days, and afterwards, the user
can wait up to 6 hours. How would you design this?
• 	S3 source images can be on 	Standard, with a lifecycle configuration to
transition them to 	Glacier 	after 60 days
• 	S3 thumbnails can be on 	One-Zone IA, with a lifecycle configuration to
expire them (delete them) after 60 days
© Stephane Maarek
NOT FOR DISTRIBUTION © Stephane
 Maarek
 www.datacumulus.com
Amazon S3 	– 	Lifecycle Rules (Scenario 2)
• 	A rule in your company states that you should be able to recover your
deleted S3 objects immediately for 30 days, although this may happen
rarely. After this time, and for up to 365 days, deleted objects should be
recoverable within 48 hours.
• 	Enable S3 Versioning 	in order to have object versions, so that “deleted
objects” are in fact hidden by a “delete marker” and can be recovered
• 	Transition the “noncurrent versions” of the object to 	Standard IA
• 	Transition afterwards the “noncurrent versions” to 	Glacier Deep Archive

content.summary:
## Storage class and retrieval constraints

Match access frequency, retrieval latency, retrieval fees, minimum storage duration and minimum billable object characteristics. Lifecycle policies should reflect the actual recovery and access pattern.

### Reasoning and trade-offs

An archival class matches long retention and tolerant restore latency, but class-specific economics and retrieval behavior must be checked. This is not appropriate when every restore must be immediate, and local instance storage does not provide an acceptable retained archive.

### Avoid this trap

Archiving all cold-looking data can violate a seconds-level restore requirement or increase cost through retrieval and minimum-duration charges. Cheapest storage is not always cheapest total access.

### Apply it

Compliance archives are retained for years and can wait hours for retrieval. They are rarely read. Which design is a reasonable starting point?

**Recommended design:** Use an appropriate S3 Glacier archival class through lifecycle rules after checking retention and retrieval requirements.

An archival class matches long retention and tolerant restore latency, but class-specific economics and retrieval behavior must be checked. This is not appropriate when every restore must be immediate, and local instance storage does not provide an acceptable retained archive.

cards.question: What should determine a storage-class transition besides the per-GB storage price?
cards.answer: Match access frequency, retrieval latency, retrieval fees, minimum storage duration and minimum billable object characteristics. Lifecycle policies should reflect the actual recovery and access pattern. An archival class matches long retention and tolerant restore latency, but class-specific economics and retrieval behavior must be checked. This is not appropriate when every restore must be immediate, and local instance storage does not provide an acceptable retained archive.

cards.question: What failure mode or trade-off must you avoid when designing storage class and retrieval constraints?
cards.answer: Archiving all cold-looking data can violate a seconds-level restore requirement or increase cost through retrieval and minimum-duration charges. Cheapest storage is not always cheapest total access.

quiz.question: Compliance archives are retained for years and can wait hours for retrieval. They are rarely read. Which design is a reasonable starting point?
options: Use an archive class for every object regardless of restore latency or retention duration.
Keep the only archive copy on a running EC2 instance-store disk.
Use an appropriate S3 Glacier archival class through lifecycle rules after checking retention and retrieval requirements.
Use Provisioned IOPS EBS solely to minimize storage cost for rarely read objects.
quiz.explanation: An archival class matches long retention and tolerant restore latency, but class-specific economics and retrieval behavior must be checked. This is not appropriate when every restore must be immediate, and local instance storage does not provide an acceptable retained archive.

## Versioning and replication are different safeguards

Versioning retains object versions and can support recovery from overwrites or deletions; replication provides another configured copy. Deletion behavior, retention, replication rules and access controls must be designed separately.

### Reasoning and trade-offs

Replication addresses copy placement; it does not by itself guarantee the desired recovery history. Versioning and retention controls protect different failure modes. Recovery must be tested against actual overwrite, delete-marker and version-deletion scenarios.

### Avoid this trap

An incorrect write or deletion can affect replicated data depending on the configuration. A second location is not automatically an immutable backup or an independent recovery policy.

### Apply it

A team enables replication and assumes every accidental overwrite can always be undone. What additional design concern should the architect raise?

**Recommended design:** Use versioning and appropriate retention or immutability controls, and test how replication handles deletes and overwrites.
